title: How Medieval Peasants Survived Winter Without Heating
thumbnail: Painterly close-up of Walter's worried face lit by a dying fire, his hand holding the last small bundle of sticks; text: '3 BUNDLES LEFT' (A/B test against a no-text version)
hook_description: How did medieval peasants survive a brutal winter with no chimney, no glass windows and no heating? Walter, a 14th-century English villager, tells you how his family lived through the great frost of 1309–1310.
character: Walter of Ashcombe, a fictional villein (unfree peasant) in an English village, winter 1309-1310
setting: Small English village of Ashcombe in the upper Thames valley, winter of 1309 to 1310

scenes.title: Tonight
scenes.narration: Tonight, the fire must not go out. If it does, my mother will not see the morning. There is snow up to the door, the woodpile is almost gone, and somebody in this village has been stealing from it. My name is Walter. And this is the longest winter of my life.

scenes.title: Three weeks earlier
scenes.narration: Three weeks earlier, the river froze. The year is thirteen hundred and nine. In London, they say, the Thames itself has turned to ice. We have no chimney, no glass, no coat of fur. So how does a family like mine survive? Let me show you.

scenes.title: Ashcombe
scenes.narration: This is Ashcombe, a village in the Thames valley. I farm fifteen acres, and I owe the lord my labour, my rent, and a hen every Christmas. But what I truly owe is this: to keep five people alive until spring. And the first secret of that is the house itself.

scenes.title: Mud and hazel
scenes.narration: Our walls are hazel sticks, woven like a basket, and plastered with daub: clay, dung and straw. It sounds poor. It is clever. Daub holds heat and stops the wind. Every autumn I fill the cracks, because a wall that whistles in November can kill by February.

scenes.title: A white roof
scenes.narration: Above us, the thatch is as thick as my arm is long. And here is something most people never guess: snow is our friend. On the roof, it seals the straw like a blanket. We never knock it off. My grandfather used to say, a white roof is a warm house. He was right.

scenes.title: The hearth
scenes.narration: Inside, everything turns around one thing: the hearth, a ring of stones in the middle of the floor. There is no chimney. The smoke finds its own way out through the thatch. It stings our eyes all winter, but it dries the roof, keeps the insects away, and cures the bacon above our heads.

scenes.title: Hook or crook
scenes.narration: The fire eats all day. The woods belong to the lord, but old custom lets us take dead wood, whatever we can pull down with a hook or a shepherd's crook. All autumn we gather branches, gorse and bundles of brushwood. Agnes counts every bundle, the way a miser counts coins.

scenes.title: The curfew
scenes.narration: And at night, we never let the fire die. We rake the embers into a heap, bury them in ash, and cover them with a clay lid called the curfew. By morning they are still alive. Relighting a fire with flint and steel, with frozen fingers, is a misery you only want once.

scenes.title: Missing wood
scenes.narration: Then, one frozen morning, I notice it. The woodpile is lower than it should be. Three bundles, maybe four. Agnes swears she has not miscounted. There are footprints in the snow, small ones, leading away toward the edge of the village. Someone is stealing our fire.

scenes.title: Dressing for the cold
scenes.narration: I say nothing yet. First, I dress for the cold. A linen shirt against the skin. Two woollen tunics. A thick hood over my shoulders. Strips of wool wound around my legs, and hay stuffed in my shoes. Wool keeps you warm even when it is wet.

scenes.title: Agnes spins
scenes.narration: Every thread I wear, Agnes spun from the wool of our four sheep. In the dark afternoons her spindle never stops. When the children outgrow a tunic, it is cut down, patched and passed on. At the very end, it becomes rags, and the rags go into the cracks of the wall.

scenes.title: Martinmas
scenes.narration: Our winter food was decided back in November, at Martinmas, when we killed the pig. There is nothing to feed a pig in winter, so it becomes bacon, sausages, lard and salt meat, packed tight in a barrel. Even the blood becomes pudding. Nothing is wasted. Nothing can be.

scenes.title: The winter store
scenes.narration: The rest of our winter lives in sacks and pots. Dried peas and beans. Onions hanging from the beams. Apples wrapped in straw. And every day, a pot of pottage over the fire, where all of it goes in together. Hot food, eaten slowly, warms you from the inside.

scenes.title: Waiting
scenes.narration: With it, dark bread of rye and barley, heavy enough to break a toe, and weak ale that Agnes brews. A cup of it, warmed at the fire, is the best moment of a winter day. But that night, I do not drink it. I take my stick, and I wait.

scenes.title: The thief
scenes.narration: Near midnight, a shape creeps up to the woodpile. It is Tom, the widow Alice's boy. No hood, no shoes, just rags tied round his feet. His father died at harvest. Their woodpile ran out a week ago. He looks at me, and he does not run.

scenes.title: The choice
scenes.narration: Taking another man's wood is a crime. Every year the manor court fines people for it, and the clerk writes their names on the roll. I could take him there tomorrow. Instead, I load his arms with two bundles, and tell him to come back on Sunday. Winter is hard enough alone.

scenes.title: The cow
scenes.narration: But generosity has a price, and in winter, everything is counted. At the far end of our house, behind a wattle fence, lives our cow. She is a great warm beast who breathes like a bellows, and she heats the house. In return, we must keep her alive until the grass returns.

scenes.title: The hay
scenes.narration: And the hay is running low. Each morning I climb to the loft, and each morning there is less. If the hay runs out, she starves, and we lose her milk and the calf in spring. Joan finds one egg today. In winter, a single egg is a feast.

scenes.title: The flail
scenes.narration: Work does not stop for cold. Three days a week I owe the lord my labour, threshing his grain in the great barn with a flail, two sticks joined by leather. Thump, thump, thump, from dawn to dusk. My shoulders burn. But the barn is dry, and hard work is warm work.

scenes.title: Christmas
scenes.narration: Then, Christmas. For twelve days, the lord's work stops. I carry my rent hen to the manor, and on Christmas Day the tenants eat in the lord's hall. We bring our own bread, a cup, and a log for his fire. And for one day, we eat meat until we can barely stand.

scenes.title: Midnight Mass
scenes.narration: At midnight Mass the church glows with candles, and I see Tom and his mother by the door, thin but alive. Alice nods to me. She says nothing. She does not need to. The priest says Christ was born in the cold too. For one night, the whole village feels warm.

scenes.title: The great frost
scenes.narration: But after Twelfth Night, the real cold comes. The ground rings like iron. A carter swears the Thames at London is frozen solid, that people walk across it and light fires on the ice. The birds fall silent. Even the well freezes. And then my mother begins to cough.

scenes.title: Three bundles
scenes.narration: Maud is old, and the cold hunts the old first. Agnes gives her warm ale with honey and sage, and we move her bed nearest the hearth. But the cough gets worse, and the fire must burn higher to keep her warm. I go to the woodpile. There are three bundles left.

scenes.title: The longest night
scenes.narration: This is the night I told you about. Three bundles, sixteen hours of darkness, and a sick old woman. If I burn it all now, we freeze before dawn. If I burn too little, Maud may not wake. So we do what peasants have always done. We use everything.

scenes.title: Warm stones
scenes.narration: First, the stones. Agnes heats flat stones at the edge of the fire, wraps them in rags, and pushes them under the blankets. They hold heat for hours, long after the flames are low. Then I pull back the cow's fence a little, so her warm breath can reach us.

scenes.title: One bed
scenes.narration: Then all of us, into one bed. A straw mattress, sheepskins and every blanket we own. Agnes and I on the outside. Joan, little Hugh and my mother in the middle, where it is warmest. Five bodies under one cover make their own fire. We sleep in our clothes.

scenes.title: Midnight
scenes.narration: In the long nights we sleep in two parts. Near midnight I wake. The fire is almost gone. I feed it one stick, and listen. Maud's breathing is slow and rough. Hugh whispers, is Grandmother going to die? I tell him to pray. So do I.

scenes.title: Dawn
scenes.narration: Before dawn, I bank the last embers under the curfew, and I must have slept, because the next thing I hear is the cock. Grey light through the shutter. And a voice, hoarse and cross: Walter, why is this house so cold? My mother is alive. I have never heard a sweeter complaint.

scenes.title: Sunday
scenes.narration: On Sunday, Tom comes back, as I told him. But he is not alone. His uncle is pulling a sledge piled with gorse and dead thornwood from the common. Enough for a week. Kindness in winter is not charity. It is how a village stays alive.

scenes.title: Candlemas
scenes.narration: By Candlemas, in early February, the light changes. The afternoons stretch a little longer. The river groans and cracks. In store we have half a sack of oats, a little bacon, a few forkfuls of hay. It is not much. But it is enough. It is always just enough.

scenes.title: Warmth
scenes.narration: You might wonder how we live without heating. But we are never without warmth. It is in our wool, our thatch, a fire that never dies, a cow's breath, and in each other. We do not fight winter. We prepare for it all year, and then we wait it out, together.

scenes.title: The fire is still burning
scenes.narration: My name is Walter of Ashcombe, and this was my winter of thirteen hundred and nine. Other winters are waiting, in Viking halls, in Roman streets, on the frozen edge of the world. If you want to live them from the inside, stay with us. The fire is still burning.
